segments.translit: jñānapānapramodena siddhācāryyo hi tāḍakas tam evārthaṃ pratipādayati —
segments.translation: Delighted by the drink of [knowledge]{jnana}, the [siddha]{siddha} master [Tāḍaka]{p-tadaka} sets out that same meaning:
segments.note: Munidatta opens: the [siddha]{siddha} master [Tāḍaka]{p-tadaka}, delighted by the drink of [knowledge]{jnana}, sets out “that same meaning”, a formula he also uses to introduce other poets. He does not say here which meaning he has in mind (cp.37.m1).

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) agrees with cp.37.m1, with rab tu tshim pa, 'fully sated', for pramoda, 'delight', and ye shes kyi btung ba, 'the drink of wisdom', for jñānapāna.

segments.translit:
apaṇetyādi | gurucaraṇareṇuprasādāt tathāgatavacanopāyadvāre[ṇa] svakāyavicāraṇātmīyasambandhaleśo 'pi mayi nāsti | ata eva āgantukaskandhakleśamṛtyumārādīnāṃ śaṅkā bhayaṃ ca me na vidyate |
tathā cāgamaḥ |
ātmaviśatītyādi |
tad idānīṃ mama tadarthavikalpabhāve mahāmudrāsiddhivāñchā dūraṃ palāyitā ca |
tathā cāgamaḥ |
naiva kvacit purā baddho 'dhunā muktir na vidyate |
bandhamuktivikalpo 'yaṃ kiñcijjñānam alakṣaṇam |
segments.translation:
“There is no [self]{atman}…” and so on. By the [grace]{prasada} of the dust of the [guru]{guru}'s feet, by way of the [means]{upaya} that is the [tathāgata]{tathagata}'s word, through [examination]{vicara} of my own body, there is in me not even a trace of any relation to what is mine. For that very reason I have no apprehension and no fear of the adventitious [aggregates]{skandha}, the [afflictions]{klesa}, the [Māra of death]{mrtyumara} and the rest.
As [scripture]{agama} says:
“The self enters…” and so on.
So now, since there is no [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} of that aim in me, my desire for the [accomplishment]{siddhi} of [Mahāmudrā]{mahamudra} has fled far away.
As [scripture]{agama} says:
“No one was ever bound before, nor is there release now. This [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} of bondage and release is limited knowledge, without a defining mark.”
segments.note: Munidatta reads 1a as fearlessness: examining his own body by the [guru]{guru}'s [grace]{prasada}, Tāḍaka finds no trace of “mine”, so he fears neither [aggregates]{skandha}, [afflictions]{klesa} nor the [Māra of death]{mrtyumara}. For 1b his paraphrase says his desire (vāñchā) for the [accomplishment]{siddhi} of [Mahāmudrā]{mahamudra} has fled far away: desire stands where the song has kaṃthā (cp.37.m2).

citations.quoted: ātmaviśati… (“The self enters…”; Tibetan bdag ni 'jug par byed)
naiva kvacit purā baddho 'dhunā muktir na vidyate | bandhamuktivikalpo 'yaṃ kiñcijjñānam alakṣaṇam

flags.note: What Munidatta's paraphrase implies for song 1b (cp.37.m2). The draft keeps কংথা as 'patched cloak' and offers 'longing' (কংখা) as the alternative. His sentence follows the line word for word: tā > tad idānīṃ, 'so now'; mahāmuderī > mahāmudrāsiddhi-, 'the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā'; kaṃthā > vāñchā, 'desire'; ṭuṭi geli > dūraṃ palāyitā, 'has fled far away'; he adds mama, 'my'. Exactly what follows: he understood the word in this place as 'desire'. That fits kaṃkhā (Sanskrit kāṅkṣā, 'longing'; kha and tha are easily confused in eastern Indian scripts), not kaṃthā. What does not follow: that his copy of the song read কংখা. He never cites the word and gives no 'X iti Y' gloss, and a paraphrase can interpret as well as read. 'Fled far away' for ṭuṭi geli (literally 'snapped, gone') also suits a desire better than a cloth, but is equally a paraphrase. The Tibetan line ('dod pa bral bar 'gyur, 'becomes free of desire') agrees on desire, but it is not independent: Toh 2293 quotes the song inside Munidatta's commentary, and its translators could follow his paraphrase. Its 'dam dang dong rtse'i, perhaps 'of mud and coin' (Sanskrit mudrā can mean 'coin'), for mahāmuderī reads that word quite differently from the Tibetan comment, which has phyag rgya chen po'i dngos grub 'dod pa, 'desire for the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā'. So Munidatta and the Tibetan support 'longing' as the sense they understood; the transmitted text, and with it the draft's 'patched cloak', is not overturned. I have not changed the draft; a note on 1b could say this.

tadarthavikalpabhāve (cp.37.m2): as written, 'in the state of conceptualizing that aim', which sits badly with the desire having fled. I translate it as if -vikalpābhāve, 'there being no conceptual thought of that aim', as the glossary entry for the patched cloak (kantha-cloak) already reads it. The Tibetan (rnam par rtog pa'i ngo bo la, 'with regard to the nature of conceptualizing') supports bhāve; on that reading the desire is itself the concept that has gone. The sense of the passage is close either way.

The last quarter of the second quotation in cp.37.m2, kiñcijjñānam alakṣaṇam, is unclear; I take it as 'limited knowledge, without a defining mark'. The Tibetan has gang de ye shes mtshan nyid min, 'that is not the mark of knowledge', as if reading na jñānalakṣaṇam.

Other places where the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads cp.37.m2 differently: (1) bdag dang bdag gi, 'self and mine', where the Sanskrit has ātmīya, 'mine', suggesting ātmātmīya, perhaps lost by haplography in svakāyavicāraṇātmīya-; (2) 'grel pa, 'commentary', evidently a slip for 'brel pa, 'relation' (sambandha); (3) som nyi za ba, 'doubt', for śaṅkā, and nothing for bhayaṃ, 'fear'. The Tibetan line 1a likewise has the tshom, 'doubt'; Munidatta's pairing śaṅkā bhayaṃ ca supports the draft's 'fear' in 1a; (4) srid pa'i don, 'the aim of existence', for tadartha, 'that aim'; the plural 'dod pa rnams, 'desires'; and shin du ring du byas, 'made very distant', for dūraṃ palāyitā, 'fled far away'; (5) the first quotation as bdag ni 'jug par byed, 'the self enters'; the Sanskrit ātmaviśati may be corrupt.

āgantukaskandhakleśamṛtyumārādīnāṃ (cp.37.m2): aggregates, afflictions, death 'and the rest' looks like the four Māras (of the aggregates, the afflictions, death, and the divine son), with -māra- applying to the whole list. The translation keeps the list as written; the glossary's Māra entry records the same reading of 'adventitious aggregates, afflictions and the like' at cp.16.m2.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena uktārthaṃ kathayati —
anubhavetyādi | ātmānaṃ sambodhya vadati, bho tāḍaka | anubhavārthaṃ kathaṃ vaktuṃ śakyate | tasmād anubhava[ṃ] sahajam iti kṛtvā kathaṃ vahasi | uta bhāvanāsaṃvṛtyānurodhena paraṃ bhanyate | na tu [54] svarūpataḥ |
tathā cāgamaḥ |
deśanīyadayogena buddho 'dvayakalpitaḥ |
paramācintayogena na buddho nāpi advayaḥ ||
tasmāc catuṣkoṭivinirmuktabhāvāt punas tena prakāreṇa tiṣṭhāmīti |
tathā cāgamaḥ |
na san nāsan na sadetyādi |
segments.translation:
With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he tells the meaning already stated:
“[Experience]{anubhava}…” and so on. Addressing himself, he says: “O [Tāḍaka]{p-tadaka}, how can the meaning of experience be put into words? So how can you maintain that experience is the [innate]{sahaja}?” Rather, it is called so only in deference to [meditation]{bhavana} and the [conventional]{samvrti}, not in its [true nature]{svarupa}.
As [scripture]{agama} says:
“By way of teaching, the [buddha]{buddha} is conceived as [nondual]{advaya}; by way of the supreme inconceivable, there is no buddha, nor anything nondual.”
Therefore: “Since my state is freed from the [four alternatives]{catuskoti}, I remain once more in just that way.”
As [scripture]{agama} says:
“Not existent, not nonexistent, not existent and nonexistent…” and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the refrain as [Tāḍaka]{p-tadaka} addressing himself, “O Tāḍaka”: the meaning of [experience]{anubhava} cannot be put into words, so how can he maintain that experience is the [innate]{sahaja}? It is called that only for [meditation]{bhavana} and convention. Freed from the [four alternatives]{catuskoti}, he remains just so (cp.37.m3).

citations.quoted: deśanīyadayogena buddho 'dvayakalpitaḥ | paramācintayogena na buddho nāpi advayaḥ
na san nāsan na sad… (Tibetan yod min med min yod med min)
citations.work: probably the Madhyamaka verse beginning 'na san nāsan na sadasan na cāpy anubhayātmakam', which calls reality freed from the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭivinirmukta, Munidatta's own word just before); ascribed to Āryadeva's Jñānasārasamuccaya, an identification from memory, unchecked

flags.note: Song 2a and Munidatta (cp.37.m3). He does not paraphrase mā bholare as such. He turns the refrain into a challenge the poet puts to himself: the meaning of experience cannot be spoken, so how can you maintain that experience is the innate? It is called so only conventionally. This reads the line as a warning against an error, taking experience, so named, for the innate, which fits the draft's 'do not be misled' (the Tibetan line's ma 'khrul, and 'khrul ma byed in 3b) better than 'do not forget', a reading that would make the line a reminder to hold on to experience as the innate, the very identification he questions. Since he gives no gloss of bhola-, this is an inference from his drift, not evidence for the word. He also takes the vocative joī, 'yogi', as Tāḍaka addressing himself (ātmānaṃ sambodhya … bho tāḍaka); in cp.37.m4 he likewise addresses 3b's joi as 'O siddha master'. The draft's 'yogi' can stand, with a note that Munidatta makes the poet his own addressee.

Song 2b says, in the third person, 'it is just as it is'; Munidatta's paraphrase (cp.37.m3) puts it in the first person, 'I remain once more in just that way' (tiṣṭhāmi), and the Tibetan comment has an impersonal gnas pa, 'abiding'. Not harmonized with the draft line; the divergence may deserve a line note.

deśanīyadayogena in the first quotation of cp.37.m3 looks corrupt. The Tibetan, tshig tu sbyor ba ston pa yis, 'by teaching through the application of words', suggests deśanāpadayogena; I translate 'by way of teaching'.
The second quotation in cp.37.m3 is cut off at na sad-… ityādi; the Tibetan gives the third member in full, yod med min, 'not existent and nonexistent', which the translation follows.

Where the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads cp.37.m3 differently: (1) rjod par byed, 'say', for vahasi, 'carry, maintain', as if reading vadasi; (2) nye bar sgom pa, 'close meditation', for uta bhāvanā, as if reading upabhāvanā; (3) kun rdzob tu mi 'gog pas gzhan la mos par byed, roughly 'by not blocking it conventionally, makes others believe', for saṃvṛtyānurodhena paraṃ bhanyate: it renders anurodha as 'not blocking' and takes paraṃ as 'others', not 'only'; (4) rab tu byed pa, the usual rendering of prakaraṇa, for prakāreṇa, 'in that way'.
“[54]” after na tu in cp.37.m3 is the manuscript's folio number; kept in the transliteration, not translated.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena tam evārthaṃ pratinirddeśayati —
jaisanītyādi | utpādakāle pavidharanairātmyābhisvaṅgāt mahāsukhamayotpanno 'haṃ mahāvajradharaḥ | punar api vajraguruṇ[ā] tasminn evā(tā)rthe dṛḍhīkṛto 'smīti tasmāt bho siddhācāryya sahaja[ṃ] pṛthak iti mā kuru | niḥśaṅkaṃ siṃharūpeṇa bhrama |
segments.translation:
With the second [verse]{pada} he points out that same meaning again:
“As you were…” and so on. At the time of [arising]{utpada}, through the vajra-holder's [attachment]{abhisvanga} to [selflessness]{nairatmya}, I arose made of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, the great [Vajradhara]{p-vajradhara}; and I have again been made firm in that very meaning by the [vajra]{vajra} [guru]{guru}. Therefore, O [siddha]{siddha} master, do not treat the [innate]{sahaja} as separate. Roam without fear, in the form of a [lion]{lion}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads “as you were” as Tāḍaka's [arising]{utpada}: through the vajra-holder's [attachment]{abhisvanga} to [selflessness]{nairatmya} he arose as the great [Vajradhara]{p-vajradhara}, made of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, and the [vajra]{vajra} [guru]{guru} made him firm in it. So the [siddha]{siddha} master is not to treat the [innate]{sahaja} as separate, but to roam fearless as a [lion]{lion} (cp.37.m4).

flags.note: pavidharanairātmyābhisvaṅgāt (cp.37.m4) can be read as 'through the vajra-holder's attachment to selflessness' (taken here), or as 'through the embrace of the vajra-holder and Nairātmā', the goddess Selflessness, a union from which the speaker arises as Vajradhara. The Tibetan has grub pa'i bdag med pa la mngon par chags pa, 'attachment to accomplished selflessness', with grub pa'i where the Sanskrit has pavidhara.

Where the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads cp.37.m4 differently: (1) nga rgyal, 'pride', for ahaṃ, 'I', making the sentence 'the pride grown into the nature of great bliss is the great Vajradhara', the deity's 'I' of tantric practice; (2) for 'I have again been made firm in that very meaning by the vajra guru' it has 'again the vajra guru teaches him the definitive meaning' (nges pa'i don), which suggests nītārthe for evā(tā)rthe and a verb of teaching for dṛḍhīkṛta; (3) lhan cig skyes pa dang tha dad ma byed, 'do not make yourself different from the innate', for 'do not treat the innate as separate'; (4) the tshom med pas, 'without doubt', for niḥśaṅkam, as for śaṅkā in cp.37.m2.

tasminn evā(tā)rthe (cp.37.m4): the parenthesis is an editorial alternative in Shastri's text. 'In that very meaning' either way; the Tibetan nges pa'i don, 'definitive meaning', might point to tasmin nītārthe.

For the song lines Munidatta paraphrases here (cp.37.m4): the Tibetan line 3b has lam, 'path', where the Bengali has pithaka, while the Tibetan comment follows Munidatta's pṛthak with tha dad, 'different'; and the Tibetan line 3a reads ji ltar 'dod pa de ltar yod par gyis, 'as you wish, so be', against Munidatta's reading of 'as you were' as the poet's arising as Vajradhara.

In cp.37.m4 Munidatta renders 3b's pithaka as pṛthak, 'separate', which supports the draft; he does not render bhānti ('confusion') or bāsa ('dwell') separately, folding them into mā kuru, 'do not treat'.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena yogīndrasya nimittam āha —
vaṇṭetyādi | yathā pārāvāre tarapatis taradānagrahaṇāya pārecchūnāṃ vāsavimokṣaṇe kaparddikānveṣaṇam api karoti teṣāṃ vaṇḍakuruṇḍādi bādhakaviśeṣañ ca paśyatīti | bāhyabhītaṃ svasaṃvedyalakṣaṇasaṃyuktaṃ [54ka] dharmmaṃ kathaṃ loke vacanadvāreṇa pratipādayitavyaṃ | tathā vākpratītidharmmādhigamāt | kṛtyādviguṇanimittaṃ lokena nirūpyate yogīndrasya |
tathā cāgamaḥ |
dhūmena jñāyate vahnir ityādi |
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he states the [sign]{nimitta} of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}:
“Vaṇṭa…” and so on. It is as at a crossing, where the [ferryman]{ferryman}, to collect his fare, even searches for [cowries]{kabadi} as those who wish to reach the [far shore]{para} loosen their clothes, and sees their particular hindrances, [vaṇḍakuruṇḍa]{bandakuru} and the like. How is a [dharma]{dharma} that lies beyond the external and is marked by [self-awareness]{svasamvedana} to be taught in the world by means of words? Even so, from his realization of the dharma, evident in his speech, and from his conduct, people make out a twofold sign of the lord of yogis.
As [scripture]{agama} says:
“Fire is known by smoke…” and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads couplet 4 as the [sign]{nimitta} of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}. As a [ferryman]{ferryman}, to collect his fare, searches passengers even for [cowries]{kabadi} and sees their hindrances, [vaṇḍakuruṇḍa]{bandakuru} and the like, so people make out a lord of yogis by signs, as fire by smoke; the [dharma]{dharma} itself, known by [self-awareness]{svasamvedana}, cannot be taught in words (cp.37.m5).

equations.en: vaṇḍakuruṇḍa and the like, named as particular hindrances of the passengers, which the ferryman sees

citations.quoted: dhūmena jñāyate vahnir… (“Fire is known by smoke…”; Tibetan du ba las ni mer shes bzhin)
citations.work: unidentified; introduced only as āgama, 'scripture'; smoke and fire is the stock example of inference in Indian logic

flags.note: What Munidatta's wording in cp.37.m5 implies for song 4a (draft: 'The ferryman knows the bāṇḍakuru'). (1) The agent is a ferryman collecting fares (tarapatis taradānagrahaṇāya), which supports the draft's 'the ferryman' for santāre, with -e as the agent ending. (2) 'Knows' is what he does when he searches the passengers and sees (paśyati) what they have. (3) The bāṇḍakuru, cited as vaṇṭa- and named in the simile as vaṇḍakuruṇḍa, is something of the passengers', listed with others ('and the like') as their 'particular hindrances' (bādhakaviśeṣa). He gives no gloss of the word. With the Tibetan snod spyad, 'vessels and implements', in both line and comment, this points to the passengers' goods or baggage (perhaps bhāṇḍa, 'wares'), but that is an inference; keeping the source form, as the draft does, is right. (4) For him the line is the vehicle of a simile (yathā … tathā): as the ferryman makes out what his passengers carry, people make out a lord of yogis by his signs, as fire by smoke; the dharma itself cannot be spoken (4b). The draft line needs no change; a line note could record this.

The word of 4a appears in three spellings: বাণ্ডকুরু in the song, বণ্ট- in Munidatta's citation (cp.37.m5) and বণ্ডকুরুণ্ড in his simile. Bengali script does not separate b and v, so his forms may as well be read baṇṭa-, baṇḍakuruṇḍa, closer to the song's bāṇḍa- than the conventional vaṇṭa- suggests; the transliteration keeps v, as the glossary does. The variation shows the word was already unstable in his text.
bāhyabhītaṃ (cp.37.m5), 'afraid of the external', makes no sense here; the Tibetan phyi'i don las 'das pa, 'beyond external objects', supports bāhyātītaṃ (or bāhyārthātītaṃ), which I translate.

The sentence tathā vākpratītidharmmādhigamāt | kṛtyādviguṇanimittaṃ lokena nirūpyate yogīndrasya (cp.37.m5) is obscure. I read tathā as completing the simile begun with yathā, and kṛtyād dviguṇa- for kṛtyādviguṇa-, with the Tibetan yon tan nyis 'gyur gyi rtags, 'the sign of doubled qualities'; viguṇa, 'faulty, without qualities', gives poor sense. I take the 'twofold sign' as the two sources just named, his realization of dharma evident in speech and his conduct; that is my construal. The Tibetan has yang dag la yid ches pa'i chos, 'the dharma of conviction in the real', where the Sanskrit has vākpratīti-, 'evident in speech'.

In the simile the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads pārecchūnāṃ vāsavimokṣaṇe as 'those who wish for liberation in the abode of the far shore' (pha rol gyi 'gro gnas su rnam par thar par 'dod pa), taking vimokṣaṇa as liberation, not the loosening of clothes, and has the ferryman 'watch their going' ('gro ba la lta bar byed) instead of searching for cowries (cp.37.m5). The glossary's hit on moksa here is the loosening of clothes, so it is not marked as 'liberation' in the translation.

tarapati (cp.37.m5), literally 'lord of the crossing', a ferry-master, is listed under the glossary's ferryman entry, so it is rendered 'ferryman'. If the reviewer wants the commentary's word to stand apart from the song's santāra, 'ferry-master' could be added as a variant.
“[54ka]” after svasaṃvedyalakṣaṇasaṃyuktaṃ in cp.37.m5 is the manuscript's folio mark (54v); kept in the transliteration, not translated.

segments.translit:
caturthapadenātyantanirvikalpatāṃ pratipādayati —
bhaṇai ityādi | siddhācāryyo hi tāḍaka evaṃ vadati | asmin dharmme bālayoginām avakāśamātraṃ nāstīti | ye 'pi paramārthavidaḥ te 'pi yadi vadanti(ti) asmābhiḥ dharmmādhigamaṃ kṛtaṃ | tadā tair eva svagrīvā saṃsārapāśena baddhā |
tathā cāgamaḥ |
tilatu sana tu viṣarṇṇa ityādi | 37 |
segments.translation:
With the fourth [verse]{pada} he sets out the state of being utterly free of [conceptual thought]{vikalpa}:
“[Tāḍaka]{p-tadaka} says…” and so on. The [siddha]{siddha} master Tāḍaka says this: in this [dharma]{dharma} there is not even room for [novice yogins]{balayogin}. Even those who know the [ultimate]{paramartha}, if they too say, “We have realized the dharma,” then they themselves have bound their own [necks]{kantha} with the [noose]{noose} of [saṃsāra]{samsara}.
As [scripture]{agama} says:
“Even a poison leaf the size of a sesame husk…” and so on. 37.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the last couplet as utter freedom from [conceptual thought]{vikalpa}: in this [dharma]{dharma} there is no room even for [novice yogins]{balayogin}, and those who know the [ultimate]{paramartha}, if they claim “we have realized the dharma”, bind their own [necks]{kantha} with the [noose]{noose} of [saṃsāra]{samsara}. He narrows “whoever understands” to those who make that claim (cp.37.m6).

citations.quoted: tilatu sana tu viṣarṇṇa… (Tibetan til dang sbun pa tsam gyi dug gi lo mas kyang, 'even by a poison leaf the size of sesame and husk')
citations.work: unidentified; introduced only as āgama, 'scripture'; its forms may be Apabhraṃśa rather than Sanskrit

flags.note: Song 5b and Munidatta (cp.37.m6). The song says only 'whoever understands has a noose round his neck'. Munidatta narrows it: the noose falls on those who know the ultimate if they say 'we have realized the dharma' (asmābhir dharmādhigamaḥ kṛtaḥ), and he names it the noose of saṃsāra (saṃsārapāśa). On his reading the fault is claiming realization, not understanding as such. The Tibetan comment agrees on 'their own neck' (de nyid kyi mgul pa) and 'the noose of saṃsāra' ('khor ba'i zhags pa), though it has 'dis, 'by this', for asmābhiḥ, 'by us', which makes the boast less explicit. The draft line keeps the song's wider wording, as it should; the narrowing belongs in the note.

Song 5a and the Tibetan (cp.37.m6): the Tibetan line reads 'Tāḍaka: there is no occasion to speak of this' ('di smra'i go skabs med), taking avakāśa as occasion to speak, while Munidatta and the Tibetan comment have no room, or no chance, for novice yogins in this dharma (byis pa'i rnal 'byor pas go skabs tsam yang med). Munidatta also reads the song's ethu, 'here', as 'in this dharma'.

The quotation tilatu sana tu viṣarṇṇa (cp.37.m6) is corrupt as printed. I translate the Tibetan, til dang sbun pa tsam gyi dug gi lo mas kyang, 'even by a poison leaf the size of sesame and husk'; the Sanskrit seems to hold tila-tuṣa, 'sesame husk', and viṣa-[pa]rṇa, 'poison leaf'. Shown as a fragment ('…and so on'); its sense, presumably that even the slightest claim is poison, is not stated by Munidatta.
vadanti(ti) (cp.37.m6): the parenthesis is editorial, probably for vadantīti, 'they say: …'; the sense is unaffected. The closing ৩৭ is the song number and is kept as '37'.

questions: Song 1b (cp.37.m2): Munidatta's paraphrase puts vāñchā, 'desire', where the song has কংথা, and the Tibetan line has 'dod pa. I read this as evidence for how he understood the word (kaṃkhā, 'longing'), not for his manuscript's reading, and the Tibetan line may simply follow his comment. Keep 'patched cloak' in the line with 'longing' in a note, or adopt 'longing'?

Song 2a (cp.37.m3): Munidatta's self-address ('O Tāḍaka, how can you maintain that experience is the innate?') reads the refrain as a warning against an error, which leans toward 'do not be misled' over 'do not forget'; but he gives no gloss of bhola-. Is that enough to settle the draft's choice, or should 'do not forget' stay as a live alternative?

cp.37.m2: I translate tadarthavikalpabhāve as if -vikalpābhāve ('there being no conceptual thought of that aim'), as the kantha-cloak glossary entry does; the Tibetan supports bhāve. Accept the emended sense?

cp.37.m5: I read bāhyātītaṃ for bāhyabhītaṃ (with the Tibetan), and kṛtyād dviguṇa- for kṛtyādviguṇa- (with the Tibetan 'doubled qualities'), taking the 'twofold sign' as speech and conduct. Is that construal acceptable, or should the sentence be translated more neutrally and flagged as obscure?

cp.37.m5 and 4a: Munidatta treats 4a as the vehicle of a simile and lists vaṇḍakuruṇḍa among passengers' 'particular hindrances'; with the Tibetan snod spyad this hints at baggage or goods. Should the bandakuru entry record the bādhakaviśeṣa classification and the b/v ambiguity of his spellings (baṇṭa-, baṇḍakuruṇḍa)?
cp.37.m5: tarapati is rendered 'ferryman' because the glossary lists it under that entry. Add 'ferry-master' as a variant so the commentary's word can be kept distinct from the song's santāra?

cp.37.m4: pavidharanairātmyābhisvaṅgāt is translated 'through the vajra-holder's attachment to selflessness'; 'through the embrace of the vajra-holder and Nairātmā' is the other reading. Which do you prefer?

cp.37.m6: the quotation tilatu sana tu viṣarṇṇa is corrupt, so I translated the Tibetan ('Even a poison leaf the size of a sesame husk…'). Is translating from the Tibetan acceptable here, or should the fragment be left in transliteration with a note?

cp.37.m3 and m4: Munidatta puts 2b in the first person ('I remain once more in just that way') and reads 3a's 'as you were' as the poet's arising as Vajradhara. Should the draft's line notes on 2b and 3a record these readings?
